articles.title: Freightos reports record booking value as transactions rise in third quarter
articles.summary: Freightos reported record booking value and higher transaction volumes in the third quarter of 2026, with both measures exceeding management expectations. The digital freight booking platform handled approximately 494,000 transactions during the quarter, up 15% from a year earlier. This was above the company’s...
articles.body: Freightos reported record booking value and higher transaction volumes in the third quarter of 2026, with both measures exceeding management expectations. The digital freight booking platform handled approximately 494,000 transactions during the quarter, up 15% from a year earlier. This was above the company’s forecast of 481,000 to 490,000 transactions. Gross Booking Value (GBV) reached a record $437 million, an increase of 30% year over year. Freightos had expected GBV of between $390 million and $397 million. The figures are preliminary and may change when the company publishes its full financial results. Freight booking activity continues to grow Freightos attributed the increase in transactions mainly to customers using its software solutions. These services connect freight forwarders, carriers and shippers through its digital booking network. The number of active carriers rose to 79, compared with 75 in the previous quarter and 77 a year earlier. The platform also recorded approximately 21,900 unique buyer users, up from 21,100 in the second quarter. Higher freight rates also contributed to the increase in booking value. According to Freightos, tight capacity and rising fuel costs affected rates during the quarter. “Our third-quarter performance reflects continued momentum across the Freightos Platform, with transaction volumes and GBV exceeding our expectations,” said Pablo Pinillos, CEO of Freightos. Full financial results expected in November Freightos provides digital booking, freight pricing and market intelligence services for international cargo transport. The company noted that its software solutions account for most of its revenue. Their performance is not fully reflected in the preliminary platform figures. Freightos will release its complete third-quarter financial results on November 23, 2026. The company will also provide further details on its software business and overall financial performance.

articles.title: Rotterdam container throughput holds steady as transshipment drops 20%
articles.summary: The Port of Rotterdam recorded a 0.9% increase in total cargo throughput during the first nine months of 2026, reaching 323.2 million tonnes. Container throughput remained largely stable, rising by 0.1% in TEU compared with the same period last year. However, container volumes measured in tonnes declined by 2.2%. The...
articles.body: The Port of Rotterdam recorded a 0.9% increase in total cargo throughput during the first nine months of 2026, reaching 323.2 million tonnes. Container throughput remained largely stable, rising by 0.1% in TEU compared with the same period last year. However, container volumes measured in tonnes declined by 2.2%. The figures also showed a sharp decline in transshipment activity, while container traffic to and from the European hinterland continued to grow. Transshipment falls as hinterland traffic increases Container transshipment at Rotterdam fell by 20% during the nine-month period. According to the Port of Rotterdam Authority, capacity constraints at deep-sea terminals have led to more cargo being handled through other ports. This has created additional space for containers moving to and from the hinterland. Hinterland container volumes increased by 7.2%, supported by an 8.9% rise in full container imports. Full container exports also grew, although at a slower rate of 1%. As imports increased faster than exports, the movement of empty containers continued to rise. Bulk cargo supports overall growth Dry bulk throughput increased by 2.1%, supported by higher coal volumes and demand for construction materials. Coal throughput rose by 15.3%, while iron ore and scrap declined by 5.9%. Liquid bulk volumes grew by 3.1%. Crude oil throughput increased by 2.1%, while mineral oil products recorded growth of 11.1%. LNG throughput edged down by 0.2%, while breakbulk volumes fell by 1.4%. Boudewijn Siemons, CEO of the Port of Rotterdam Authority, highlighted the importance of reliable transport connections as European trade flows continue to change. “Reliable infrastructure is the basis for economic growth and a resilient supply chain,” said Siemons. The port authority stressed the need for continued investment in road, rail and inland waterway connections to support European trade and improve supply chain resilience.

REUTERS/Ints Kalnins ANKARA, Oct 18 (Reuters) – Turkey will take some of the diesel Russia is supplying to global markets under its agreement with US President Donald Trump, Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said on Sunday. Bayraktar said the US-Russia diesel supply deal was important in terms of energy security for Turkey. Ankara relies on Russia for some of its energy needs, as well as on Iran, Azerbaijan and others. It is trying to diversify through deals with the US and other partners. “Russia imposed restrictions on diesel exports in recent months when they started experiencing this problem. Now they reached a diesel deal with Trump… Through the talks we held, we will take some of that diesel to Turkey,” Bayraktar told broadcaster Kanal 7. He did not elaborate. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European officials and some of Trump’s fellow Republican politicians strongly criticized the deal. Bayraktar also said that Turkey plans to bring a second floating gas production platform online in the first quarter of 2028, adding that the platform would bring Turkey’s daily output in the Black Sea to 45 million cubic meters. On Saturday, Turkey sent its first floating gas production platform, the Osman Gazi, to the Black Sea, a move Bayraktar has said is expected to roughly double daily output from its largest domestic gas field, the Sakarya field, to 20 million cubic meters from the current 9.5 million, equivalent to 7.3 billion cubic meters (bcm) annually. “In the first quarter of 2028, the second floating production platform is coming to Turkey and we will carry out 25 million cubic meters of production with it. It has a slightly bigger capacity (than Osman Gazi),” he said. “Therefore, with 45 million cubic meters, we will be using our own gas in three out of four homes in Turkey.” He added that Turkey’s daily production at the field would increase to 550,000 barrels of oil equivalent with the second floating platform. Turkey is one of Europe’s largest gas markets, consuming 59 bcm last year. The country relies on imports for almost all its gas needs, with domestic production totalling 3.1 bcm last year, most of it from the Sakarya field. Bayraktar also said hydrocarbon exploration operations planned off Pakistan had been delayed by about six months due to the Iran war’s impact on the region. articles.body: Tankers: Is a Clean Slate Coming for 15% of the Tanker Fleet? in Hellenic Shipping News 19/10/2026 A sudden boost of tanker supply could emerge, should the US proceed with a waiver of sanctioned tankers. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Gibson said that “the US is weighing a waiver that would let tankers sanctioned for links to Russia, Iran or Venezuela carry non-sanctioned oil, or be sold to mainstream owners, in a bid to bring down record freight rates and move more crude and products out of the Middle East Gulf. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said high freight has hurt demand for US crude. Owners would apply to the US Treasury, cases would be reviewed individually, and the waiver would cover the ships, but not Russian or Iranian oil”. According to Gibson, “some 878 tankers, 15% of the trading fleet, are under sanctions, rising to 25% for Aframax/LR2s. The US can only waive its own designations, however, and EU and UK cooperation looks unlikely. That leaves 325 tankers listed by OFAC alone as the possible pool, and 153 of them are VLCCs, covering almost all of the 164 sanctioned VLCCs. Only 28 of the 116 sanctioned Suezmaxes and 42 of the 322 Aframax/LR2s are OFAC-only, and clean tonnage is limited, as around 40 CPP MRs, mostly in the East, potentially available for mainstream trade. 84% of OFAC only tankers are in the Middle East, Indian Ocean or Far East, with just 16 individual ships in European waters, so any direct impact would be felt East of Suez. Atlantic charterers would benefit only indirectly, if sanctioned tonnage takes market share in the East and pushes more mainstream ships to ballast West”, the shipbroker said. Source: Gibson Shipbrokers Ltd Gibson added that “Iran directly owns 64 sanctioned vessels of which 38 VLCCs, and more are possibly held by Iranian interests in other jurisdictions. Where links to the IRGC exist, OFAC may be reluctant to grant waivers. Chinese and Hong Kong owners hold a further 43, which could in theory look to trade in the Middle East. 70% of OFAC-listed tankers are 20 years or older, including 120 of the 163 VLCCs. The conflict has made age less of a barrier, but without IG P&I cover and IACS class, few charterers will be able to take these ships. Their most likely employment is on Hormuz shuttle runs, where the recent increase in attacks has constrained supply. Iranian-linked vessels may be less exposed to attack, though the US Navy will be monitoring for any ship trying to breach the blockade”. Meanwhile, “mainstream buyers could also seek approval to purchase sanctioned tonnage, and the extra ships available could weigh on secondhand values. Russian exporters may face higher freight costs if some of their trading tonnage is drawn into Middle East business. The length of any waiver matters too, as a short-term reprieve may not be enough for charterers to commit to longer voyages, and the risk of renewed tensions after next month’s midterm elections may further limit appetite”, the shipbroker said. It added that “the waiver could add capacity to the Hormuz shuttle trade in particular and could have some freight impact across the wider market. Most of the tonnage it could add is old, mostly VLCCs, sitting East of Suez. Since any delisting would follow OFAC’s usual full review, it may take time for a significant number of ships to be freed for mainstream trade. The TD3C VLCC FFA market has corrected downwards over the past couple of days, in part due to this news. In the end, the number of waivers given out will decide whether any impact is felt at all”, Gibson concluded. The rate for the transatlantic route of 70,000mt US Gulf/UK Continent (TD25) lost 203 points to the WS755 mark, which gives a round-trip TCE basis Houston/Rotterdam of $234,851. On the Vancouver export routes, rates are mixed, with owners showing a preference for longer voyages over shorter trips. articles.body: Dry Bulk Market: Capesizes Declined Slightly Last Week in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 19/10/2026 C apesize The market endured a sustained and broad-based decline through the week, with the BCI 182 5TC falling from $37,618 at Monday’s close to $29,464 by Friday. Persistent selling pressure across both basins drove rates lower, with sentiment deteriorating as the week progressed. The Pacific remained under pressure throughout, with limited miner participation and insufficient fresh enquiry to support rates. Despite a brief increase in C5 miner activity midweek, competition among owners intensified as bids retreated, with fixtures falling from $13.40 at the start of the week to $11.25 by Thursday. However, the return of two miners on Friday provided some support, prompting greater resistance from owners and allowing the C5 index to recover to close the week at $11.70. The Atlantic also weakened, with increased fixing activity later in the week in the South Brazil and West Africa to China markets, albeit at progressively lower levels. C3 index-date business slipped towards $30, reflecting ample tonnage supply and limited buying appetite. The North Atlantic remained subdued, with weaker transatlantic and backhaul fixtures adding to the negative sentiment, while activity on the Fronthaul route remained limited. Panamax-Kamsarmax The week opened with a largely balanced Atlantic market, where a steady flow of mineral cargoes supported transatlantic activity, although sufficient vessel availability continued to limit any meaningful upside. A 75,000-dwt vessel was reported fixed for a US Gulf transatlantic trip at $21,500. Meanwhile, sentiment in the Pacific improved on active demand from Australia, Indonesia and the North Pacific, with reports of prompt tonnage tightening and firmer fixing levels. A 76,000-dwt fixed an Indonesia trip to South China at $18,000, a 93,000-dwt fixing for a North Pacific round at $20,000, and an 82,000-dwt fixed for an Australia round trip at $19,000. By midweek, the divergence between the two basins became more pronounced. While Pacific demand remained supportive, Atlantic sentiment deteriorated as tonnage accumulated, particularly in the North Continent and South Atlantic. Charterers tested lower levels amid widening bid-offer spreads, limited grain demand and growing concerns over vessel oversupply. Although the Pacific remained comparatively resilient, easing East Coast Australia enquiry later in the week prompted suggestions that rates had reached a near-term ceiling. Period activity remained evident, particularly for laden legs and short period employment. An 82,000-dwt fixed for two laden legs trading within the Atlantic at $27,000, a 94,000-dwt fixed two to three laden legs basis delivery in the Pacific at $24,000 and a 75,000-dwt fixed for five to seven months at $19,000. With the exception of Monday, the P5TC declined throughout the week, with the steepest losses recorded towards the end of the week. Ultramax/Supramax The index saw slow gains throughout the week driven mainly by the Asian market. The US Gulf started on a steady footing with a 63,000-dwt fixed US Gulf to China with petcoke at $34,000, but rates later softened as surplus tonnage took effect. The south fared better with a 63,000-dwt fixed Santos to Ain Sukhna with sugar redelivery Port Said at $36,000 and fronthaul levels flat around $19,250 plus $925,000 ballast bonus, which was in line with last week. The Continent, however, peaked last week against scrap demand, but levels remain strong albeit lower and the Mediterranean finally saw more activity with a 63,000-dwt fixed passing Canakkale to West Africa with clinker at $22,000. The North Pacific witnessed slow and steady gains continuing from last week and a newbuilding 63,000-dwt fixed from Kunsan via NoPac to Indonesia at $25,000 and backhauls also increased with another similar newbuilding fixed ex yard Zhoushan at $29,250 for a trip to the Mediterranean, whilst a 63,000-dwt fixed from North China to West Africa at $24,000. Southeast Asia was also more active and rates to India saw the most improvement, however there was very few period trades rumoured throughout the week, despite the continued strength. Handysize The Handysize market delivered a mixed performance across the regions this week. The Continent and Mediterranean remained stable, supported by a healthy cargo book. A 37,000-dwt open Hereke 10–12 October was fixed passing Canakkale via Iskenderun to the North Coast of South America at $11,000. In the South Atlantic, market fundamentals remained strong, particularly for larger vessels, indicating continued support. A 36,000-dwt was placed on subjects for a trip from Santos to the West Coast of South America at $31,500, and a 39,000-dwt was said to have fixed at $32,000 for EC South America to the Continent. By contrast, the US Gulf remained sluggish, with limited activity and a continuing downward trend driven by an oversupply of tonnage. A 35,000-dwt was reported fixed from SW Pass to the West Coast of Central America with grains at $17,500. Meanwhile, the Pacific firmed amid tight tonnage and healthy demand from the North Pacific and Australia. A 37,000-dwt vessel open Port Kelang 11–13 October was fixed via Australia to China at $16,000. Source: Baltic Exchange Tops 2026-10-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Faster Ballast, Slower Laden: VLCC Supply Signals Diverge
articles.summary: This week’s Tanker Market Monitor examines divergence in VLCC sailing speeds, regional vessel supply, and freight earnings. In the Arabian Gulf, ballast vessels are accelerating while laden ships are slowing, with no clear improvement in overall voyage turnaround. Meanwhile, the western VLCC ballast surplus has...
articles.body: Faster Ballast, Slower Laden: VLCC Supply Signals Diverge in International Shipping News 19/10/2026 T his week’s Tanker Market Monitor examines divergence in VLCC sailing speeds, regional vessel supply, and freight earnings. In the Arabian Gulf, ballast vessels are accelerating while laden ships are slowing, with no clear improvement in overall voyage turnaround. Meanwhile, the western VLCC ballast surplus has narrowed, in contrast to rising ballast numbers East of Suez. Despite this increase in eastern vessel supply, Gulf VLCC earnings remain exceptionally high, and dirty-tanker freight continues to outperform the clean market by a substantial margin. The findings highlight why faster repositioning and higher ballast counts have yet to translate into meaningful freight relief. Arabian Gulf VLCC ballast speed reached 12.00 knots, up 2.5% from the previous week, while laden speed declined 5.5% to 11.52 knots, leaving ballast vessels sailing 0.48 knots faster than loaded ships. The current speed-implied supply indicator stood 3.7% above its 90-day average, reflecting faster repositioning rather than an increase in available tonnage. While this may shorten ballast voyages, slower laden sailings, waiting times and cargo transfers continue to affect vessel turnaround, with no clear evidence yet of improved effective VLCC availability. MARKET SIGNAL: Western VLCC availability tightened, with the ballast surplus down 23.7%, but the combined at-sea balance did not: a larger eastern surplus left it 2.1% higher. Freight performance split sharply by vessel class, with all four assessed Suezmax routes up on the week and all five western Aframax routes down. Dirty Freight Outpaces Clean Tankers The Baltic Dirty Tanker Index (BDTI) rose 32% to a Week 41 average of 7,625 points, significantly outpacing the 2% increase in the Baltic Clean Tanker Index (BCTI) to 2,388 points. VLCC freight on the Arabian Gulf–China route (TD3C) also strengthened, averaging WS1,288, up 12% from the previous week. By 14 October, the BDTI stood at 7,922 points, easing from its 13 October peak of 7,999, the highest reading in the supplied 12-month series and almost seven times its level a year earlier. The modest pullback leaves crude tanker freight at historically elevated levels, with little indication of a meaningful reversal in the recent upward trend. Freight: Gulf VLCC Earnings Lead as Atlantic Aframax Rates Ease VLCC: In the 15 October snapshot, Gulf routes still carry the highest earnings in the crude basket. MEG–Singapore (TD2) stands at $1,412,730/day, flat on the week, and MEG–China (TD3C) at $1,356,523/day, down 2.8%. AG–China earnings remain 86.0% above West Africa–China (TD15, $729,311/day, -4.0%) and 124.8% above US Gulf–China (TD22, $603,486/day, -2.0%). Over the month, however, the Atlantic routes rose faster: TD22 is up 108.2% and TD15 65.3%, against 31.1% for TD3C. All four assessed Suezmax routes recorded weekly gains. Black Sea–Mediterranean (TD6) rose 11.7% to $903,854/day, now above MEG–Mediterranean (TD23) at $765,675/day (+1.3%). West Africa–UK Continent (TD20) added 3.1% and Guyana–ARA (TD27) 1.8%. All five western Aframax routes fell, while both eastern routes increased. US Gulf–ARA (TD25) dropped 14.0% to $273,166/day, East Coast Mexico–US Gulf (TD26) 13.3% to $337,127/day and Caribbean–US Gulf (TD9) 10.8% to $307,313/day. East of Suez, SE Asia–East Coast Australia (TD14) rose 19.2% to $271,465/day, the largest weekly gain in the basket, and Kuwait–Singapore (TD8) gained 3.0%. In total, nine of the 16 dirty routes declined week on week. All 16 routes remain above their month-earlier levels, with gains ranging from 31.1% to 276.6%. VLCC Supply Tightens West of Suez as Eastern Ballast Numbers Rise West of Suez, ballast vessels declined 6% to an average of 56, reducing the ballast surplus by 24%, from 8 to 6 vessels. East of Suez, ballast numbers increased 4% to 192, outpacing the rise in laden vessels and lifting the regional surplus by 6% to 49. By 14 October, western laden VLCCs outnumbered ballasters for the first time since mid-August, while eastern ballast numbers continued to rise. The latest figures point to tighter vessel positioning in the Atlantic, against a larger pool of ballast tonnage in the East that has yet to ease exceptional Gulf freight earnings. Average VLCC counts declined across western regions in Week 41, led by Europe (−26.3%, from 41 to 30), the Atlantic Ocean (−12.8%, from 45 to 39) and the Americas (−9.8%, from 68 to 62). In contrast, counts increased in the Middle East Gulf (+3.8%, from 189 to 196) and Indian Ocean (+6.9%, from 70 to 75). The shift points to a greater concentration of VLCCs in eastern waters, although total vessel counts do not necessarily reflect prompt availability for charter. China Congestion Edges Higher but Stays Below Last Year China’s VLCC waiting count averaged 12 vessels in Week 41, up 14% from the previous week, while vessels at port remained close to seven. The combined average increased 7% to 19 vessels, with the rise concentrated in the waiting queue. Congestion remained below the same week of 2025, when an average of 14 VLCCs were waiting, and 9 were at port. By 14 October, the daily count had eased to 9 waiting vessels, while 8 were at port, pointing to some moderation in the waiting queue. Hormuz Freight Watch: Bunker Supply Tightens as Saudi Delivered Sales Expand Marine fuel availability remains constrained across key bunkering hubs, while Saudi Arabia expands delivered crude sales to Asian refiners. Renewed attacks in Hormuz continue to complicate vessel deployment and loading arrangements. Bunker fuel constraints: Marine fuel availability remains tight across several East of Suez locations. In Singapore, recommended lead times have extended to 11–18 days for VLSFO and 11–17 days for HSFO. Fujairah has seen some improvement in VLSFO availability, although HSFO and LSMGO supplies remain limited. Port Suez is also reporting critically low inventories across conventional bunker grades. These constraints add to voyage planning requirements, particularly for vessels operating between the Gulf, Red Sea and Asian discharge ports. Saudi delivered crude sales: Chinese refiners purchased at least 12 million barrels of Saudi crude for November loading on a delivered basis, with additional sales to India and Taiwan. Buyers’ reluctance to charter vessels for loading inside Hormuz has encouraged Saudi Arabia to arrange transportation directly, while allocations continue through Yanbu and Sidi Kerir. This keeps crude moving but transfers responsibility for securing tanker capacity to the seller. Hormuz security: UKMTO reported projectile strikes involving a tanker and container ship on 13 October. Singapore’s maritime authority separately confirmed that GFS Pride was struck and subsequently sank, while GFS Giselle sustained damage and reached safe anchorage following an attack on 14 October. These incidents reinforce the continuing uncertainty surrounding Gulf transits. Source: By Maria Bertzeletou, Signal Group, https://www.thesignalgroup.com/weekly-market-monitor/weekly-tanker-market-monitor-week-41-2026 Tops 2026-10-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: In the Arabian Gulf, ballast vessels are accelerating while laden ships are slowing, with no clear improvement in overall voyage turnaround.
Meanwhile, the western VLCC ballast surplus has narrowed, in contrast to rising ballast numbers East of Suez.
Despite this increase in eastern vessel supply, Gulf VLCC earnings remain exceptionally high, and dirty-tanker freight continues to outperform the clean market by a substantial margin.

articles.title: nOn Cyber Extortion Incident Involving 38 Maritime Companies Likely traces Back to a Single Vendor
articles.summary: On 12 October 2026, the cyber extortion group n0n listed a batch of 38 maritime organizations on its dark web leak site. The targets include shipping companies, port terminal operators, container operation companies, logistics companies, ship managers and agents, and other maritime-related companies in 18 countries....
articles.body: nOn Cyber Extortion Incident Involving 38 Maritime Companies Likely traces Back to a Single Vendor in International Shipping News 19/10/2026 On 12 October 2026, the cyber extortion group n0n listed a batch of 38 maritime organizations on its dark web leak site. The targets include shipping companies, port terminal operators, container operation companies, logistics companies, ship managers and agents, and other maritime-related companies in 18 countries. The listings carry ransom demands ranging from USD 400 thousand to 400 million per company, almost all with the same deadline: 19 October 2026, 13:27 UTC. Cydome’s research team analyzed the available information on this incident and assessed that it is likely linked to data from CyberLogitec, a Korean company that provides software and IT services to maritime companies. At least 21 of the 38 companies are publicly documented CyberLogitec customers, and other details in the 85 sample files published by n0n also point to CyberLogitec as the source. While we continue to analyze the incident, our interim assessment is that the stolen data may come from a single source, a support and project archive that originated at, or is linked to, CyberLogitec and relates to its customers. Rather than 38 different breaches, n0n appears to have split the data into separate “victims” parts and set an individual ransom demand for each customer. This is not confirmed, and reflects what the available information shows so far. We do not know which system was accessed, how, or how much of each customer’s data was taken. We checked the available data, and while we cannot validate its authenticity, we have indications that the stolen data contains sensitive information, such as passwords and personal information. Some of it is dated to several years ago, so it is not necessarily current. Everything in this analysis should be read as alleged. Key Findings • On 12 October 2026, n0n listed 38 maritime organizations in 18 countries, with demands totaling about USD 1.22 billion and a common deadline of 19 October 2026, 13:27 UTC. • At least 21 of the 38 victim organizations are publicly documented CyberLogitec customers, and 7 sample file names include the vendor’s name or one of its product names. • Our interim assessment is that the data likely comes from a single support and project archive linked to CyberLogitec, split into separate listings per customer. • The samples indicate credentials, personal data, EDI traffic and system documentation, with file dates from 2009 to August 2026. • Being named on the list does not necessarily mean an organization’s own network was breached. Who Is n0n n0n first surfaced on 18 September 2026. The researchers who documented the group reported that it gets in with credentials stolen by infostealer malware. Several of its September listings were service providers whose listings advertised their clients’ data, in industries such as financial services, technology, retail and education. Some threat intelligence vendors list n0n as likely Russia-based, but we have not seen the evidence behind this assessment, and we do not attribute the group to any country (although, there is some evidence that they are not related to Iran, Chine or North Korea). The October 12 Maritime Listings The maritime listings appeared in a single batch on 12 October, according to ransomware.live. Names on the list include the likes of Ocean Network Express, Pusan Newport, BNCT, Santos Brasil, TTI Algeciras, Eurogate Tanger, NEOM Ports and ZPMC. In South Korea, BoanNews reported that KISA, the national cyber agency, notified the Korean companies on the list. Dongkuk Steel told NGetNews it could not confirm actual damage. Korean logistics outlet Daily Log reported that CyberLogitec confirmed the named Korean companies are its customers and sent them a precautionary notice, and that their systems are operating normally. n0n has followed through on earlier deadline threats. On 13 October, it replaced several anonymous listings with the victims’ real names within hours of their deadlines passing. We suggest treating the 19 October deadline as a real threat. As a side note, most of the deadlines are listed to be at 13:27 UTC, with one at 13:19 UTC. This corresponds to verses from the Gospel of John, where Jesus tells Judas Iscariot at the Last Supper, right after Satan enters him, “What you are about to do, do quickly,” [13:27] and “Now I tell you before it come, that, when it is come to pass, ye may believe that I am he.” [13:19]. This could be an indication that the n0n group is Christian in origin. Tracing the Common Source to CyberLogitec CyberLogitec and Its Products CyberLogitec is a Seoul-based maritime and logistics software company. It belongs to EUSU Holdings, a Korean holding group that also owns EUSU Logistics, one of the listed organizations. Terminal operators, container lines, bulk and tanker operators and logistics companies use its software: • OPUS Terminal is a terminal operating system (TOS). Terminal operators use it to plan berths, vessels and yard space, control container moves and gate transactions, and bill their customers. OPUS Terminal M is a cloud version for smaller terminals. • ALLEGRO is a liner operations system for container ship lines. It covers bookings, bill of lading documentation, container and equipment management, vessel schedules and billing. • OPUS Bulk manages voyages for dry bulk and tanker operators, from voyage estimates and chartering to operations, laytime, demurrage and voyage accounting. • CARA is a cloud service that container lines use to review and manage special cargo, such as out-of-gauge cargo and dangerous goods. • OPUS D&D calculates and invoices demurrage and detention charges, based on each carrier’s tariffs and free time. The company also provides IT infrastructure managed services and EDI management to port terminals, and runs a 24/7 global service desk through its Vietnam subsidiary. It reports more than 150 customers worldwide. The materials published by n0n include specific references to CyberLogitec, along with what appear to be customer emails, support tickets, sample EDI files, release notes and other correspondence typical of customer support. Customer Overlap We checked each organization on the list against press releases, trade press and EUSU Holdings investor materials. Figure 1. Relationship of each listed organization to CyberLogitec. Source: Cydome research, October 2026 · based on press releases, trade press and EUSU Holdings investor materials The documented customers span 9 countries and all of the products mentioned earlier. File names on two more listings refer to CyberLogitec or its products. CyberLogitec has a large share of the Korean market, so some of the Korean overlap could be coincidence, but the list also includes its customers in Brazil, Spain, Morocco, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia. To our knowledge, so far CyberLogitec has not confirmed an incident in this case. Sample File Analysis Each listing includes 2 or 3 sample files. We reviewed the names of all 85. The main ones are below. Table 1. Selected sample file names from the n0n maritime listings Listing Sample file (as published) What the name suggests BKH ICD (CLT-OTM) Release Note_PKT_20250327.pdf A vendor release note that names CyberLogitec (CLT) and OPUS Terminal M Eurogate Tanger EGT_Release Note_Release_OPUS Terminal_20230707.docx A release note for the vendor’s OPUS Terminal product Pusan Newport Deploy List(2024-04-08) (UAT).xlsx A deployment list for a test environment Kambara Kisen Allegro Seacast CSV June.2024 Refers to the vendor’s ALLEGRO product CULines CUL-ALG-ITO_CULSD-4053_FS_v1.0.docx A functional specification with a ticket key Asyaport ASYM-1747_01ADD-COLUMN-TOSADM… .sql A database patch script with a ticket key TTI Algeciras Enhancement – [EDI] COPRAR – Decimals in weight A support request for an EDI change Figure 2. Leak-site listings for CULines and Ocean Network Express, as captured by ransomware.live. CULines’ sample files reference the vendor’s ALLEGRO product. ONE’s listing carries a $400 million demand. Some file name patterns repeat across customers in different countries. 7 file names include the vendor’s name or one of its product line names. Several carry what appears to be ticket keys made of a customer code and a number. Table names in files from Turkey and Korea follow the same naming convention. Many names end with a 5-digit sequence, which is consistent with an export from a ticketing or mail system. The dated file names run from 2009 to August 2026. In one case, a listing reuses a file from another listing. GlobalNet LCL’s listing includes the same sample file as the April Asia listing, with the same catalog number and an identical description. This suggests that being named on the list does not always mean an organization’s own data was taken. Assessed Data Exposure Based on the file names, the listing descriptions and our review of the available data, we found indications that the archive could include: • Credentials and personal data. We have indications that the data includes user account lists with passwords, and staff details such as names, email addresses and phone numbers. These examples are dated from 2018 to 2022, so they are not necessarily current. Some listings also refer to infrastructure records, such as server and network information, from several years ago. • EDI traffic. Stowage plans (BAPLIE), bookings (COPARN), gate moves (CODECO) and loading lists (COPRAR). These messages often carry data about other carriers. One terminal’s sample includes a gate-move file for ONE, and Yusen’s includes HMM tariffs. • System and implementation material. Release notes, deployment lists, data migration specifications, interface specifications and database patch scripts. These reveal system versions, table structures and interface details. • Commercial records. Tariffs, invoices, charter parties, port disbursement accounts and demurrage calculations. Note that these are indications only. We cannot confirm the scope of the breach or the authenticity of the information, although we did not find any flaws that would indicate fake data. Even outdated information can be misused. People often reuse passwords or change them only slightly, and real names, roles, and email addresses make phishing messages more convincing. Exposure may also reach beyond the 38 names. Carriers and partners whose messages pass through a listed terminal could appear in the data without being listed. Ransom Demand Structure Each listing shows a settlement amount, its individual bitcoin address (for payment), and a one-time option to pay 10% of the full ransom price to open a negotiation room. Across all 38 listings, the demands add up to about USD 1.22 billion, with individual listings ranging from USD 400,000 to 400,000,000. Figure 3. Advertised demand per listing Source: n0n leak site via ransomware.live, 13 to 15 Oct 2026 · all 38 maritime listings 4 listings carry demands of USD 100 million or more: Ocean Network Express ($400 million), Apical Group ($320 million), ZPMC ($160 million) and Dongkuk Steel ($100 million). The amounts rise with company size, regardless of what the sample files contain. Some figures reported in the Korean press, such as $10 million for Dongkuk Steel, match the 10% negotiation option rather than the full demand. Assessed Attack Scenario and Open Questions One explanation that fits the evidence so far is a single archive from CyberLogitec’s support environment, split by customer name. n0n used a similar approach in September, when it listed service providers along with their clients’ data. This is still a hypothesis. Figure 4 marks the steps that are not verified. Figure 4. Assessed attack scenario. Cydome assessment, October 2026 · hypothesis, not a confirmed sequence n0n is a new group, first seen less than a month before this batch. We do not know whether it stole the data itself or acquired it from a third party, for example, by buying it from other hackers. The file dates range from 2009 to August 2026. Older material could have been taken earlier and later sold or passed on, so both options remain open. Open questions remain: which system held the data (the vendor’s own, or a third-party ticketing or mail platform), who took it and how, and how much of it relates to each named organization. Recommendations for Maritime Operators We recommend that maritime organizations: 1. List every vendor support and remote-access account, including shared service-desk logins, and rotate shared or long-lived credentials, especially passwords that have not changed in years. 2. If you use CyberLogitec products, review admin and integration accounts in those systems first. 3. Review CyberLogitec account activity from July 2026 onward. File names refer to dates as recent as August 2026. 4. Warn operations, IT and finance teams about targeted phishing. Real ticket numbers, engineer names, EDI samples and invoice templates make convincing lures. This is true even if your organization is not on the list, as those details may be hidden within the stolen data. 5. Check what your organization has sent to software vendors, especially CyberLogitec, by email or tickets over the years. Look for sensitive information such as credentials, network diagrams, database exports and configuration files. 6. Require MFA on vendor portals and service-desk access, and add breach notification terms to vendor contracts. 7. If your organization is named, do not treat the listing as proof that your own network was breached. Establish where the data came from before responding to any demand. 8. Monitor IT and OT networks for unusual activity, so that misuse of leaked configuration or credentials is caught early. Cydome’s maritiem cyber experts are available to support with responding to, or preventing, this threat. Conclusion Software vendors that serve ports and carriers often hold years of support correspondence, EDI configurations, billing data and user lists for their customers. If one of their support environments is compromised, many customers can be exposed at once, even if their own networks were never touched. We saw a similar pattern in the second wave of the Lab Dookhtegan campaign, where disruption across many tankers traced back to a single satellite service provider, and in previous incidents where a breach at a single maritime service provider affected the operations of many of its customers. Cydome is following this campaign ahead of the 19 October deadline. If you work with any of the named organizations or use CyberLogitec systems, book a short exposure review with our team. Source: Cydome 2026-10-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Asia-US container rates mixed as extended peak season demand wanes; tanker rates stable in International Shipping News 19/10/2026 Rates for shipping containers from east Asia and China to the US were mixed this week while rates for liquid chemical tankers ex-US Gulf were largely stable. CONTAINER RATES Container rates were mixed this week to both US coasts. Rates to the West Coast are between $7,475-8,300/FEU (40-foot equivalent unit) while rates to the East Coast are between $9,600-11,300/FEU, remaining near the highest since mid-2022 for both routes. Rates from supply chain advisors Drewry rose by 3% from Shanghai to Los Angeles while rates from Shanghai to New York fell by 1%, as shown in the following chart. Drewry said it expects rates to be less volatile next week as capacity is expected to be stable amid management via blank sailings. Drewry also said that persistently strong import demand from the US continues to support rates at current levels. Rates from ocean and freight rates and analytics firm Xeneta edged slightly lower and it anticipates continued downward pressure, as shown in the following chart. “Spot rates from the Far East to the US have remained almost flat for the past month, but we are now in mid-October and through Golden Week, so downward pressure is expected to intensify,” Emily Stausboll, senior shipping analyst at Xeneta, said. “The telling signal is that carriers are removing capacity, with 58,200 TEU (20-foot equivalent unit) blanked on the Far East to US West Coast trade this week and 35,500 TEU from Far East to US East Coast,” Stausboll said. Stausboll said actions take by carriers seem to indicate their belief that these higher rates are not sustainable. “When spot rates on US trades are still up triple-digit percentages compared to pre-Hormuz crisis in February, carriers would normally be adding capacity rather than blanking sailings, so this looks like the behavior of carriers who don’t believe the market will hold and are protecting the current level rather than expecting further growth,” Stausboll said. Rates from online shipping marketplace and platform provider Freightos fell by 2% to the West Coast and were flat to the East Coast. Judah Levine, head of research at Freightos, said rates have been supported at current levels by sustained peak season demand together with congestion at Asian ports. He said that this week’s decrease could signal the start of a downward trend with Golden Week behind us. The National Retail Foundation (NRF) projects November arrivals to drop 11% month on month, suggesting that peak season is finally coming to an end and that rates may ease until demand pressure from the pre-Lunar New Year rush kicks in late this year or starting in January. Rates on the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI), which tracks rates for containers leaving Shanghai, rose by 0.04%, the second weekly increase after falling for the previous two weeks. Rates on the NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) rose by 0.9% to the West Coast and rose by 1.1% to the East Coast. Container ships and costs for shipping containers are relevant to the chemical industry because while most chemicals are liquids and are shipped in tankers, container ships transport polymers, such as polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP), which are shipped in pellets. Titanium dioxide (TiO2) is also shipped in containers. They also transport liquid chemicals in isotanks. LIQUID CHEMICAL TANKERS US chemical tanker freight rates assessed by ICIS were steady this week with rates remaining unchanged week on week despite continuing to face downward pressure for several trade lanes. Rates from the USG to ARA trade lane remain unchanged; however, demand along this route continues to be slow following EPCA, leading to further downward pressure on rates, despite somewhat limited open available space. Overall, the market remains balanced, while demand from the region continues to be dominated by methanol and caustic soda, with several large parcels being fixed. There continues to be downward pressure on rates along the USG-Asia trade lane as charterers are still in wait-and-see mode pending port tariff issues between US and China. Besides contract of affreightment (COA) cargoes, there is very little seen in the market. However, COA volumes continue to be the only bright spot, as several cargoes have already been diverted to other ports. Although on a spot basis, any activity along this lane has been mainly focused on methanol. From the USG to Brazil, this trade lane remains unusually quiet and in turn rates increased on the high end of the range and fell on the lower end. Fewer fixtures were noted this week; the lack of prompt availability seems to be somewhat tight and therefore owners appear to be cautious about letting rates decline any further. Several parcels of caustic soda and acetic acid were reportedly fixed for first half of October dates. The USG to India route has seen fewer inquiries over the last week with a few confirmed fixtures. There was only one new quote seen for October and November dates. However, along with the other regions, freight rates are widely viewed as softer. Most market players are trying to reposition cargoes and vessels to avoid the China route. Overall, most of the activity has been focused on methanol and a variety of easy chemicals. articles.summary: Japan is set to provide protection and indemnity cover and partially compensate cargo and hull insurance payments for the transportation of crude oil, oil products and LNG, as part of a bill approved by the Cabinet on Oct. 13, a senior official at the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry said. articles.body: Japan to provide P&I, compensate cargo, hull cover for crude, oil products, LNG transport in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 19/10/2026 Japan is set to provide protection and indemnity cover and partially compensate cargo and hull insurance payments for the transportation of crude oil, oil products and LNG, as part of a bill approved by the Cabinet on Oct. 13, a senior official at the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry said. The bill is one of three approved by the Japanese Cabinet earlier Oct. 13 to enhance the security of the country’s crude oil supply, among others, amid the conflict in the Middle East. “The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism will revise the existing specified tanker act. The current law covers crude oil, and the scope will be expanded to include petroleum products such as naphtha, as well as liquefied natural gas,” the METI official told a press briefing. METI will also introduce similar support measures for hull insurance and cargo insurance, the official added. In response to the Middle East situation and to ensure a stable supply of energy to Japan, METI said the government will establish a program under which it will partially compensate non-life insurance companies for the funds required to pay insurance claims under marine property insurance, such as cargo and hull insurance, covering the transportation of crude oil, oil products and LNG, even in cases where the provision of reinsurance is prohibited. “In the event foreign insurance companies become unable to provide reinsurance coverage, a situation could arise where the cargo is available but cannot be transported,” the official said. “To address such circumstances, the government will establish a mechanism to fill the gap left by the unavailable foreign reinsurance coverage.” Japan introduced a law in 2012 to compensate P&I cover as a sovereign guarantee for each tanker carrying Iranian crude amid EU sanctions against Iran — an initiative that remains in effect to date. However, Japan suspended its imports of Iranian oil in May 2019. The Japan P&I Club, formally known as the Japan Ship Owners’ Mutual Protection & Indemnity Association, provides insurance cover of up to about $9.8 billion per tanker. METI Minister Ryosei Akazawa said earlier Oct. 13, “Today, the Cabinet approved three bills: a bill concerning the rationalization of the use of designated sea lanes to ensure the stable transportation of crude oil among others; a bill on special measures to secure the fulfillment of specified cargo insurance contracts and specified vessel insurance contracts; and a bill to partially amend the Act on the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security.” “In light of the structural changes taking place in the global energy landscape, including the recent situation in the Middle East, it is necessary to strengthen the resilience of Japan’s energy supply and demand structure,” Akazawa told reporters. “Through these three bills, we aim to fundamentally enhance the stability of procurement by diversifying the sourcing of crude oil and other fossil fuels and reducing associated risks,” he added. The Cabinet’s approval comes after Japan formulated an energy policy package on Aug. 26, under the direction of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, to bolster the resilience of the country’s energy supply and demand system through Green Transformation (GX) initiatives known as POWERR GX. Other bills The first bill, which concerns the rationalization of the use of designated sea lanes to ensure the stable transportation of crude oil and oil products, importers such as refiners, petrochemical producers and trading houses will receive grants when they procure crude oil and oil products from suppliers located outside the Strait of Hormuz region, the official said. To receive the grant, these companies will be required to formulate a designated sea lane rationalization plan that sets out details such as procurement targets, the types of crude oil covered, shipping routes and the duration of the plan, the official added. The government will then review and certify the plan, after which JOGMEC will provide grants covering a portion of the costs associated with supply diversification, the official said. The funding for these grants will come from contributions paid by refiners and other importers, which JOGMEC will use to finance the grant program, the official added. Regarding the bill amending the JOGMEC Act, the official said the recent situation in the Middle East has underscored the critical role that alternative pipelines can play in ensuring Japan’s crude oil procurement. The proposed measure would allow JOGMEC to provide equity investments and debt guarantees for such pipelines, which are not associated with specific oil and gas fields, as it can currently provide equity investments and debt guarantees only for pipelines associated with oil and gas fields, the official added. As part of the amendments to the JOGMEC Act, JOGMEC’s mandate will also be expanded to include equity investments and debt guarantees for projects involved in overseas biofuel production, the official said. “Demand for biofuels and other alternative fuels is expected to increase due to regulations in Japan and overseas,” the official said. “It is important to ensure ample supply so that biofuel supply and demand can be brought into proper balance.” JOGMEC’s functions will also be expanded to include equity investments and debt guarantees for smelting and refining projects that process used materials, such as spent batteries and other recyclable metal resources, the official said. JOGMEC will also be given the additional function of administering subsidy programs for carbon capture and storage projects, the official said, adding that the subsidies will be provided in accordance with grant criteria established by METI and are intended to support projects by addressing the gap between CCS costs and the prevailing carbon price. articles.body: Biofuel Bunker Snapshot: Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO premium over VLSFO narrows in International Shipping News 19/10/2026 Europe Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO (POMEME) price has gained $36/mt in the past week, while the Dutch port’s conventional VLSFO price has jumped $54/mt over the same period. This has narrowed Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO price premium over conventional VLSFO by $17/mt, to $174/mt. Dutch suppliers can generate ZRE A tickets for selling low-carbon fuels, which can be traded with other suppliers. The price of these tickets held at €240/mtCO2e ($269/mtCO2e) on Thursday this week, unchanged from last Thursday. These ZRE A tickets help lower Rotterdam’s biofuel prices compared with other ports. Belgium has no such mechanism. articles.summary: Vessels transit the Hormuz Strait off the coast of Iran’s southern port city of Bandar Abbas on September 7, 2026. Commercial vessels are likely to continue navigating the perilous Strait of Hormuz despite the sinking of a Singapore-flagged container ship this week, as strong demand for Middle Eastern energy and...
articles.body: One Singapore ship was sunk, but here’s why others are still transiting the Strait of Hormuz in International Shipping News 19/10/2026 Vessels transit the Hormuz Strait off the coast of Iran’s southern port city of Bandar Abbas on September 7, 2026. Commercial vessels are likely to continue navigating the perilous Strait of Hormuz despite the sinking of a Singapore-flagged container ship this week, as strong demand for Middle Eastern energy and lucrative shipping opportunities keep some operators willing to brave escalating attacks, maritime experts said. The latest attacks on two Singapore-flagged container ships have heightened concerns over the safety of commercial shipping through one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints. But analysts say the incidents are unlikely to bring remaining shipping activity through the Strait to a halt, even as major container lines largely stay away. Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said shipping companies were likely to continue seeking opportunities to transit the strait despite heightened security threats. “I don’t see in the short term, that Singapore flagged ships or Singapore shipping companies would necessarily avoid taking the transit if there is an opportunity,” Koh told CNBC. His comments follow attacks on two Singapore-registered container ships, GFS Pride and GFS Giselle, this week. GFS Pride sank after being struck by a projectile and catching fire, while GFS Giselle was damaged. Crew members from both vessels were reported safe. Crossings through the Strait of Hormuz fell to 131 in the week ended Oct. 14, from 176 the previous week, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler, although the decline cannot be attributed solely to the latest incidents. Dimitris Ampatzidis, maritime risk and compliance manager at Kpler, said the attacks underscored Iran’s continuing ability to threaten commercial vessels, with the risks extending beyond oil and gas transportation. Commercial incentives persist Koh said shipping companies around the world have continued looking for opportunities to navigate the Strait since the conflict erupted, with some operators prepared to accept higher risks and costs. Strong demand for oil, particularly from Asia, continues to provide an incentive for tanker operators to transport energy supplies from the Persian Gulf, even as security threats complicate voyages. Some operators may be willing to take their chances even if doing so involves paying a premium, Koh said. Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan offered an example of how higher oil prices could make voyages through Hormuz commercially worthwhile despite the dangers. Speaking at the Milken Institute Asia Summit last week, Balakrishnan recounted a conversation with an unnamed Gulf counterpart who said his country was earning more from oil exports than before the war by operating a so-called “Hormuz shuttle” involving about 20 very large crude carriers. The vessels were effectively self-insured against attacks, according to the official’s account, with higher crude prices making the voyages financially worthwhile despite the risks. “Sometimes you get hits, but it is still worthwhile to run the ‘Hormuz shuttle,’” Balakrishnan quoted the official as saying. Despite the risks, vessels continue to transit the Strait, reflecting its commercial importance, particularly for energy shipments to Asian markets, Ampatzidis said. However, further attacks could deter more operators from making the passage, with the impact likely to differ depending on vessel type and individual companies’ assessments of the risks, he added. The Singapore Shipping Association also played down the prospect of a broad withdrawal of commercial shipping from the region, suggesting operators would instead adapt to changing trade conditions. “Rather than signalling a broad withdrawal from the region, these developments are more likely to result in adjustments to trading patterns as markets respond to shifts in the supply and demand of goods and energy,” said association president TS Teo. Shipowners would continue weighing commercial considerations against security developments and crew safety when making operational decisions, he added. Wider shipping disruptions While some operators remain willing to transit Hormuz, much of the global container shipping industry has already adjusted its networks to avoid the strait. Jayendu Krishna, a director at Drewry Maritime Advisors, said none of the major container shipping lines had resumed services through Hormuz since suspending operations following the outbreak of the war in February. Only some regional operators have continued sporadic services, generally using smaller feeder vessels. That means the immediate impact of the latest attacks on container shipping could be limited, he said. However, a further escalation into the Gulf of Oman could pose a more serious threat to regional supply chains, particularly if it disrupts alternative ports like Khorfakkan in the United Arab Emirates and Oman’s Sohar that have become critical gateways for cargo entering Gulf countries. “If the Gulf of Oman became a zone of kinetic activity, a significant part of supplies to the Gulf countries would be cut off, since Khorfakkan and Sohar have been a lifeline for them,” Krishna said. articles.title: Trade Data vs. Maritime Intelligence: What Customs Agencies Actually Need
articles.summary: Trade Data Was Built for Commercial Visibility Cargo manifests, customs declarations, shipping records, and import and export filings exist to describe commerce. They do that well. How much crude moved through Yanbu last month? Which companies are shipping dry bulk into Rotterdam? What do the dominant trade flows...
articles.body: Trade Data vs. Maritime Intelligence: What Customs Agencies Actually Need in International Shipping News 19/10/2026 Trade Data Was Built for Commercial Visibility Cargo manifests, customs declarations, shipping records, and import and export filings exist to describe commerce. They do that well. How much crude moved through Yanbu last month? Which companies are shipping dry bulk into Rotterdam? What do the dominant trade flows look like across the Red Sea corridor this quarter? These are real questions with real answers, and the platforms built to answer them serve commodity traders, banks, and supply chain managers properly. Those are not the questions customs enforcement asks. Enforcement Asks a Different Set of Questions Which of the 15,000 containers arriving at this port today holds something that was not declared? Which vessel took a detour through a sanctioned port before arriving here? Which manifest is fraudulent? Which operator has a behavioral history that signals concealment? Trade data does not answer any of these, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of coverage or refresh rate. Trade data is a record of what parties declared. The enforcement problem begins at the point where the declaration stops being true. AIS does not close the gap either. A vessel running dark produces no AIS record to check. A vessel broadcasting manipulated positions produces a record that is worse than nothing, because it looks complete. In both cases, the vessel most worth examining is the one generating the least usable data. That is the shape of the enforcement problem. The subject of the investigation controls the inputs. Intelligence Starts Where Declarations Stop All-source maritime intelligence fuses the layers that exist independently of what a vessel or operator chooses to declare. EO and SAR satellite imagery sees a vessel whether or not it is transmitting. SAR works through cloud and darkness, so coverage does not depend on conditions. RF detection identifies a vessel’s emissions signature when AIS is off, because a ship running dark is still operating equipment that radiates. Behavioral analytics built on years of vessel activity flag deviations no single manifest could reveal. A route that does not match the stated voyage. A loitering pattern in a corridor associated with transfer activity. A dark period that begins and ends in places that make the gap itself the signal. Ownership and entity resolution surfaces the beneficial owner behind layers of flag hopping and shell structures, which is how an operator with a history of concealment appears as the same operator rather than as a new company with a clean record. Fused, these produce an intelligence picture rather than a data feed. The distinction matters operationally. A feed tells an officer what was reported. A picture tells them what happened, with enough specificity to justify an inspection. Container Targeting Shows the Gap Most Clearly Container targeting is the sharpest illustration. Trade data can tell you that a container is declared as machine parts from a legitimate exporter with a clean filing history. Every field checks out. On a declaration-based targeting model, it ranks low and passes. Trade data can tell you that a container is declared as machine parts from a legitimate exporter with a clean filing history. Every field checks out. On a declaration-based targeting model, it ranks low and passes. When UK authorities seized roughly $100 million of cocaine from a container ship at London Gateway, the public reporting named almost nothing. A container vessel, a Panama port call, a June arrival. Those three details were enough to run a search, returning three vessels that matched the profile during the relevant window. One carried a documented history, surfaced automatically through adverse media screening, of a 2016 case in which approximately 200 pounds of cocaine were found concealed in a container loaded at Santos. The vessel’s European port call sequence, June 2025. Source: Windward Maritime AI™ Platform. The routing is the part a declaration cannot show. Panama in early June, across the Atlantic, Antwerp on June 21, Rotterdam on June 23, London Gateway on June 25, then onward to Germany. Each leg generated its own paperwork, and each set of paperwork was accurate. The shape of the voyage, and the vessel’s own history, are what carried the signal. All-source intelligence can tell you that the vessel carrying it called at a sanctioned port three legs ago with AIS switched off, that the declared exporter shares ownership infrastructure with entities already under sanctions, and that the vessel’s behavioral pattern in the week before loading matches a known concealment sequence. None of that is visible in the declaration. All of it is available before arrival. That is the difference between a declaration and an intelligence product. A declaration describes an intention. An intelligence product describes a history. Customs officers allocating finite inspection capacity need the second one, because the first was written by the party they are assessing. The timing compounds the advantage. Declarations arrive close to arrival, leaving a narrow window to act. Vessel behavior accumulates across the entire voyage, which means the risk picture can be built while the ship is still at sea. What Do You See When the Vessel Switches Off? That is the test, and it is worth applying to any source an agency relies on. Trade data sees nothing. The declaration describes the leg that was filed, not the voyage that happened, and it arrives regardless of what the vessel did in between. AIS sees nothing. That is the point of switching it off. All-source intelligence still has a picture. Satellite detection places the vessel. RF confirms it. Behavioral models read the gap itself as an indicator rather than a blank. Ownership intelligence connects the operator to everything else it controls. With all-source operational intelligence, whatever an agency needs to complete the picture comes in alongside the rest, whether that is national holdings, partner reporting, industry data, or a source specific to the mission. Concealment is not an edge case in customs enforcement. It is the case. A targeting model that performs well on cooperative vessels and loses sight of uncooperative ones is optimized against the wrong population. The vessels that matter most are the ones that stopped reporting. What an agency can see during those windows determines what it can stop. Swedish Coast Guard/Handout via TT News Agency/via REUTERS By Karin Matussek Oct 18, 2026 (Bloomberg) –A Ukrainian army officer suspected of being a protagonist in the sabotage of Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022 stood trial in Hamburg accused of committing a war crime. The man, identified as 50-year-old Serhii K., was chosen by Ukraine authorities to lead the operation, prosecutor Stefan Schmidt said on the first day of trial. Serhii K. was arrested in Italy a year ago and extradited to Germany. “He had the mandate and authorization from the Ukraine government,” prosecutor Schmidt said. The crucial pipelines ferried gas from Russia through the Baltic Sea to Lubmin, a costal city in the North East of Germany. Serhii K. was an officer in the Ukrainian Army. After Russia invaded the country in February 2022, he and other military personnel, acting on behalf of Ukrainian government agencies, devised a plan to destroy the Nord Stream 1 and 2 natural gas pipelines , according to the indictment. The goal was to permanently halt gas deliveries via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from gas trades to finance its war efforts. To carry out the plan, Serhii K. allegedly lead a group of professional divers, a boat captain skipper and an explosives expert. In early September 2022, the crew entered a sailing yacht which had been rented in Rostock, Germany, using forged identification documents. With the ship, the men transported explosives for military use to a location near the Danish island of Bornholm. In the weeks leading up to the attack Serhii K.’s group attached various explosive devices with time fuses to the pipelines. They detonated on September 26, 2022. Serhii K.’s lawyers rejected the allegations. Nicola Canestrini, a defense lawyer for Serhii K., said Germany can’t try his client for a war crime because that wasn’t covered by the Italian extradition ruling granted only for a sabotage charges. No one was hurt or killed by the incident and Germany tragically mistakes who the real perpetrators are, Canestrini told the court. “After Bucha, Mariupol, and the abducted Ukrainian children, he’s the first person the German authorities are trying as a war criminal—not a Russian, but an officer in the armed forces defending against a war of aggression,” he said. Russia had used the pipeline as a military, financial and political weapon in the war , so defining it as a merely civilian object was wrong, he added. There was also no direct evidence, like finger prints or DNA, that proved Serhii K. was on the yacht, Canestrini said. The indirect evidence prosecutors are now citing was illegally transferred from Italy to Germany without proper judicial authorization. Serhii K.’s lawyers asked the court to drop the case because his Ukrainian military superiors didn’t allow him speak about details of his service and disclosing them would be a crime under Ukrainian law. Since he can’t properly defend himself now, the trial must be discontinued, they argued. Speculation had swirled about the origin of the attacks on the pipelines, installed to deliver natural gas from Russia to Germany under the Baltic Sea. The incident triggered a wave of accusations, with Russia blaming it on sabotage by the US, Ukraine and Poland, calling them “beneficiaries” of the blasts. The Nord Stream 1 undersea link to Germany was the main route for Russian pipeline gas flows before the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, while the second pipeline was completed but never went operational. In 2021, the year before the war started, Nord Stream 1 delivered more than a third of Russia’s total gas exports to Europe. Razieh Poudat/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS DUBAI, Oct 18 (Reuters) – Iran’s offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday. Iran presented its proposal in mid-September after an interim ceasefire collapsed . Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response but Iran’s security chief said last week negotiations have stalled because Washington failed to address all seven conditions for reopening the strait. “Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn’t, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious,” Araqchi said while in Baghdad for a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Iran’s conditions include, among other demands, the lifting of the US blockade on its ports, the lifting of US sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts. If Washington accepts Tehran’s conditions, the strait could reopen within six days, with talks resuming the following day, Araqchi said. A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran’s nuclear program from the outset. US Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries’ eight-month war. Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz , which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security in the waterway. Bulgarian Interior Ministry/Handout via REUTERS BUCHAREST, Oct 17 (Reuters) – Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country’s territorial waters on Saturday, the defense ministry said. The drones were brought down days after two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania’s Black Sea coast, the latest in a series of attacks highlighting risks to commercial shipping on NATO’s eastern flank. Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal , which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is an export route for Ukraine. NATO member Romania shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, and has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Romania started shooting down such drones earlier this year. The defense ministry said the two drones entered Romanian waters in the Black Sea on Saturday at 1459 GMT and 1501 GMT, respectively. The ministry did not specify the origin of the drones. The two tankers struck earlier this week were hit by Russian drones, a NATO military source told Reuters. Romanian officials are still searching for seven missing crew members . At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighboring Bulgaria in the past 10 days, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents occurred outside NATO territorial waters. In Moldova, on Romania’s northeast border, officials said a new drone had crashed in a northern district, near the border with Ukraine. Officials said there were no casualties or damage and specialists were trying to determine the drone’s origin. The number of drones violating Moldovan airspace has increased greatly in recent months. Five drones identified as Russian fell on Moldovan territory in a little more than 17 hours on Thursday and Friday, prompting the foreign ministry to issue a statement denouncing Russian actions. articles.title: Wind-Assisted Shipping Gains Ground as Airbus RoRo Adds Rotor Sails
articles.summary: French shipowner LD Armateurs has completed the installation of six towering rotor sails aboard Spirit of Toulouse, a new roll-on/roll-off vessel being built to transport aircraft components for Airbus across...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Caption: LD Armateurs’ Spirit of Toulouse, built for Airbus transatlantic transport operations, fitted with six 35-meter-tall Norsepower rotor sails at an outfitting site in Shanghai, China. Photo: LD Armateurs/Norsepower French shipowner LD Armateurs has completed the installation of six towering rotor sails aboard Spirit of Toulouse , a new roll-on/roll-off vessel being built to transport aircraft components for Airbus across the Atlantic. The installation, completed at a shipyard outfitting site in Shanghai, makes the 168-meter vessel the largest RoRo ship equipped with wind-assisted propulsion and gives it more mechanical sails than any other ship, according to LD Armateurs and Finnish wind propulsion specialist Norsepower. Each of the six rotor sails stands 35 meters tall and measures 5 meters in diameter. The rotating cylinders harness wind to generate additional thrust, reducing the workload on the ship’s main engines and, in turn, its fuel consumption. The vessel is also equipped with two dual-fuel main engines and two generator sets capable of operating on e-methanol, bio-methanol or marine diesel oil. The combination is intended to reduce fuel consumption and emissions without relying entirely on alternative fuels. Spirit of Toulouse is the first of three sister ships being built for LD Armateurs under charter to Airbus. The other two vessels, Spirit of Mobile and Spirit of Mirabel , will also receive six rotor sails each. The ships will transport large aircraft assemblies between Airbus production facilities in Europe and North America, replacing the manufacturer’s existing transatlantic fleet. Airbus expects the new fleet to cut annual emissions from its transatlantic shipping operations by more than half, from approximately 68,000 metric tons of CO2 in 2023 to 33,000 metric tons by 2030. Those reductions will depend on a combination of improved vessel efficiency, wind propulsion and the availability of lower-emission fuels. “Completing installation of six Norsepower Rotor Sails on Spirit of Toulouse is a significant milestone for wind propulsion in the RoRo segment,” said Heikki Pöntynen, CEO of Norsepower. The vessel was launched in February and is preparing for sea trials, during which the rotor sails will undergo testing. Further adjustments are planned during its maiden voyage from China to France. Wind Propulsion Gains Ground The project comes as wind-assisted propulsion moves beyond individual demonstration projects and finds wider use across the commercial shipping fleet. According to the International Windship Association (IWSA) , more than 100 large commercial vessels were equipped with wind propulsion systems as of June 2026, carrying more than 230 individual installations. That compares with just 21 large vessels in May 2022, representing nearly a fivefold increase in four years. Tankers and bulk carriers have led the expansion, although RoRo ships, ferries and general cargo vessels are increasingly adopting the technology. Earlier this year, Berge Bulk completed the installation of four folding rotor sails on its 208,000-dwt Newcastlemax bulk carrier Berge Meru , following a similar project aboard the larger Berge Neblina in 2024. In August, the Ultramax bulk carrier Maria Topic returned to commercial service after receiving a rigid wingsail during a retrofit at Tsuneishi Shipbuilding in Japan. And in September, Spanish shipowner Marflet Marine installed four 22-meter suction sails aboard the 49,999-dwt chemical tanker Santiago I , with technology supplier bound4blue estimating the system could reduce annual energy consumption by approximately 10% to 15%. The growing range of installations reflects the different approaches being used to capture wind energy. Rotor sails use spinning cylinders to generate thrust through the Magnus effect, while other systems employ rigid wings, suction sails or even kites. Unlike conventional sailing vessels, most wind-assisted merchant ships continue to rely on their main engines for propulsion, using wind power to reduce fuel consumption whenever conditions allow. The technology has also produced measurable results. In an earlier trial involving the Maersk Pelican product tanker, two Norsepower rotor sails delivered an independently validated 8.2% reduction in fuel consumption over one year. More recently, Cargill reported that the bulk carrier Pyxis Ocean , fitted with two large WindWings, achieved average fuel savings of approximately three metric tons per day during a six-month trial. With two more Airbus vessels to follow, the project will provide another test of how those technologies perform together in regular commercial service.
