Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS Conflicting traffic figures and competing claims of control are making it increasingly difficult to establish what’s happening in the Strait of Hormuz, even as attacks on merchant shipping intensify. The true extent of attacks on merchant ships in the Strait of Hormuz remains unclear, with a new report from UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) acknowledging that most vessels struck in the region are not reporting incidents directly to the maritime security organization. The admission comes as the United States and Iran offer sharply different accounts of who controls the vital waterway, while conflicting transit figures raise further questions about how much commercial shipping has actually recovered. In its weekly overview published Friday , UKMTO said it is struggling to establish the true number of attacks because the majority of vessels targeted are refusing to submit reports. UKMTO said it is aware of additional incidents through other sources but cannot include them in its reporting without sufficient verification. The disclosure raises questions about the reliability of publicly available attack statistics, particularly following a sharp escalation in strikes against commercial vessels over the past two weeks. UKMTO recorded 12 attacks during its latest reporting period, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz, one in the Arabian Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. Six vessels continued their voyages or reached port, two were disabled or left not under command, and three had unconfirmed damage or outcomes. One vessel, the Singapore-flagged containership GFS Pride , was lost after being struck by a projectile. The report also found that 55 of 74 documented projectile strikes since July 6 occurred along the southern route through the strait, accounting for nearly three-quarters of the reported attacks. The findings stand in contrast to increasingly confident statements from U.S. military officials about their control of the waterway. In a video statement Friday, Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, said American forces and regional partners remain firmly in control of the strait despite continued Iranian attacks. “Let me be clear: the Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran. And it remains open for business,” Cooper said. He reported that approximately 400 merchant ships had transited the strait over the preceding seven days, while U.S. forces helped Gulf partners move more than 100 million barrels of crude oil during the same period. Cooper said those shipments added to more than 1.3 billion barrels of crude transported with U.S. assistance in recent months. But the latest UKMTO figures paint a different picture. For the seven days ending October 14, UKMTO recorded 254 combined transits, including 129 inbound and 125 outbound movements. That was down from 275 the previous week, with traffic remaining approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels. Of those 254 movements, just 42 were observed through Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. The remaining 212 were drawn from U.S.-reported facilitated transits, which include ships operating without broadcasting AIS. UKMTO cautioned that the U.S.-supplied figures and associated totals cannot currently be independently verified. Cooper did not specify the exact dates covered by his 400-transit figure, leaving open the possibility that the difference reflects separate reporting periods or counting methods. Nevertheless, the gap illustrates the difficulty of establishing a consistent picture of commercial traffic through the strait. Iran, meanwhile, continues to dispute Washington’s account of control over the waterway. Iranian army chief Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami said Thursday that the strait would remain closed until the rights of the Iranian people were respected. The latest Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) advisory , published October 15, describes both a northern Iranian-controlled route and a southern Omani corridor, while warning that ships operating with AIS switched on face an elevated risk of targeting and instructions to divert toward the Iranian route. UKMTO’s latest report adds that most vessels broadcasting AIS continue to use the Iranian route, even as U.S.-facilitated traffic accounts for the majority of reported transits. The competing accounts reflect the increasingly complicated security environment for merchant shipping. U.S. forces are facilitating substantial traffic through the strait, while Iran continues to demonstrate an ability to strike vessels, including those using the southern corridor. And with UKMTO now acknowledging that most attacked vessels are not reporting incidents directly, even the growing number of documented strikes may offer only a partial picture of the dangers facing seafarers. International Seaways has agreed to acquire Oslo-listed Bruton Limited in a deal valued at approximately $370 million, adding four very large crude carriers (VLCCs) to its fleet as tanker earnings remain elevated. The New York-based tanker owner announced the agreement Friday, saying the acquisition will expand its fleet of approximately 70 crude oil and product tankers. The deal includes one VLCC already in operation and three newbuildings under construction at China’s New Times Shipyard. The acquisition comes alongside preliminary financial results showing strong tanker market conditions. International Seaways reported average blended spot earnings of approximately $68,000 per day during the third quarter, more than double the $29,000 per day recorded a year earlier. Rates have climbed further entering the fourth quarter. The company said it has secured blended spot earnings averaging approximately $180,000 per day for about 37% of its expected fourth-quarter revenue days. Under the acquisition agreement, International Seaways will initially acquire a 50.5% stake in Bruton through a share exchange with existing shareholders, expected to settle around October 20. The company will then acquire the remaining shares through a cash-and-stock merger. International Seaways expects to issue approximately 3.12 million shares as part of the transaction, accounting for roughly 96% of the total consideration. The remainder will be paid in cash. Bruton shareholders are scheduled to vote on the merger around October 30, with the transaction expected to close shortly afterward, subject to customary conditions. “We’re excited about the opportunity to expand and modernize our fleet through this accretive transaction with Bruton,” said Lois K. Zabrocky, president and CEO of International Seaways. “The transaction underscores our disciplined approach to growth.” Bruton’s fleet consists of the 300,000-dwt Mount Vision, delivered in July, and three sister vessels scheduled for delivery between November 2026 and October 2027. According to Bruton’s fleet information, Mount Vision is earning $95,000 per day under its existing charter, while the next vessel, Mount Horizon, has secured a charter at $105,700 per day. Bruton previously controlled a larger VLCC newbuilding program, but spun off eight vessels into OMC Tankers, which began trading in Oslo in August. Those eight newbuildings are not part of the International Seaways acquisition. International Seaways also expects third-quarter revenue of $480 million to $490 million and net income of $340 million to $350 million, including an approximately $50 million gain from the sale of a 2012-built Suezmax tanker. The company reported liquidity of approximately $965 million at September 30, including $455 million in cash and short-term investments. Its full third-quarter financial results are scheduled for release on November 5. articles.title: UK ports hit back at Brussels over ETS diversion claims
articles.summary: British ports have challenged European Union claims that shipping lines are diverting container traffic to the UK to escape carbon charges, warning that proposed anti-evasion measures risk penalising billions of pounds of investment in British terminals. The British Ports Association (BPA) has rejected findings from...
articles.body: Environment Europe Operations Ports and Logistics Regulatory UK ports hit back at Brussels over ETS diversion claims Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 1,432 3 minutes read UK Government UK Government British ports have challenged European Union claims that shipping lines are diverting container traffic to the UK to escape carbon charges, warning that proposed anti-evasion measures risk penalising billions of pounds of investment in British terminals. The British Ports Association (BPA) has rejected findings from Spain’s EU ETS Observatory linking rising UK container activity to the bloc’s Emissions Trading System, arguing that new capacity, changing liner networks and commercial competition offer more convincing explanations. In a new report, the association said around 85% of the UK’s container traffic growth in 2025 was concentrated in London, following the opening of DP World’s £350m ($465m) fourth berth at London Gateway in late 2024. Government figures show UK ports handled 11% more containers last year, equivalent to an additional 600,000 units. London accounted for roughly 500,000 of those, with its growth driven largely by the additional capacity at London Gateway. The DP World terminal handled more than 3m teu in 2025, up 52% from 1.9m teu a year earlier. The increase followed the opening of the fourth berth, which boosted capacity by more than a third, and the arrival of Asia-Europe services operated by Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd’s Gemini Cooperation in February 2025. London Gateway has been challenging Felixstowe’s position as Britain’s busiest boxport, with Maersk’s departure from the Hutchison-operated facility reshaping the country’s container market. DP World is pressing ahead with another £1bn ($1.33bn) expansion, adding two all-electric berths and a second rail terminal. The BPA argues that such investment and network changes have been overlooked in assessments linking Britain’s expanding container business to EU carbon pricing. The dispute follows research by Spain’s Puertos del Estado, which found the UK’s share of northern European deepsea shipping activity, measured in teu-miles, rose from 17.5% in 2023 to 32.1% by July 2025. Subsequent analysis put the figure at around 36% in the first quarter of 2026, broadly mirroring declines in Germany and the Netherlands. The Spanish study also estimated that 76% of observed route changes were attributable to the EU ETS, raising concerns that containerlines were restructuring their networks to reduce carbon costs. But the BPA has questioned both the methodology and the conclusions. It argues that teu-miles, which combine vessel capacity with voyage distance, measure shipping network activity rather than actual containers handled. The metric can also be distorted by longer voyages around the Cape of Good Hope and changes to the sequence of port calls. The association also disputes treating the widely cited 76% figure as evidence of carbon-driven diversion specifically to Britain, arguing that the available analysis does not isolate the effects of ETS from alliance restructuring, congestion and new terminal capacity. Continental European ports have not uniformly lost ground either. Rotterdam’s container throughput increased 3.1% to 14.2m teu in 2025, Hamburg recorded 7.3% growth to 8.3m teu, while Antwerp-Bruges posted a 0.7% increase. The disagreement comes after the European Commission proposed tightening rules designed to prevent containerships from using neighbouring non-EU ports to reduce their ETS exposure. Under proposals unveiled in July, certain container ports within 150 nautical miles of an EU port could be excluded from the definition of a port of call for emissions accounting purposes. The threshold for transhipment activity at other qualifying non-EU ports within 300 nautical miles would also be lowered from 65% to 50%. The changes could bring more British terminals within the EU’s anti-evasion framework, potentially increasing carbon costs for shipping lines using them. The proposals have yet to be adopted. “It would be extraordinary if the EU responded to that success by introducing new measures to penalise British ports,” said Mark Simmonds, the BPA’s director of policy and external affairs. The association stressed that it supports shipping decarbonisation but warned against treating normal competition between ports as regulatory avoidance. Britain has already brought domestic shipping and emissions in UK ports into its own emissions trading scheme from July this year, while plans to extend carbon pricing to international voyages from 2028 are also under consideration. The BPA has urged the UK government and the European Commission to reassess the evidence before proceeding with measures that could affect port competitiveness and future investment on both sides of the Channel. The agreement, announced on Friday, will see the Lois Zabrocky-led group acquire Bruton’s entire four-ship supertanker portfolio, going considerably further than the sale of two newbuildings first linked to the US owner in market reports last week. International Seaways has secured agreements with shareholders representing 50.5% of Bruton, including Trøim’s Drew Holdings and Koch Inc, to exchange their holdings for newly issued shares in the US company. The exchange is set at 0.0519 International Seaways shares for each Bruton share, with the initial transaction expected to settle around October 20. The remaining shares will be acquired through a merger, with Seaways expecting to issue approximately 3.12m new shares, accounting for 96% of the total consideration. Smaller Bruton shareholders will receive cash at $6.3044 per share. The deal brings four 300,000 dwt VLCCs into the Seaways fold, including the LNG dual-fuel Mount Vision , which entered service in July, and sistership Mount Horizon , scheduled for delivery from China’s New Times Shipbuilding next month. The remaining two vessels, Mount Frontier and Mount Summit , are due in August and October 2027. The first two ships already have substantial charter cover. Mount Vision secured a 3+1+1-year arrangement with a trading house, earning $95,000 per day for the initial nine months before switching to an index-linked structure. Mount Horizon has been fixed for 12 to 15 months at $105,700 per day. The two 2027 newbuildings remain unchartered and have been at the centre of the recent sale speculation. Splash detailed the potential deal last week after Bruton acknowledged market rumours and launched a strategic review. At the time, International Seaways was linked to the purchase of at least two newbuildings, with brokers discussing values north of $200m per vessel. Bruton’s own figures put the original yard cost of the two 2027 ships at about $117m apiece, highlighting how sharply modern VLCC asset values have moved. The $370m announced on Friday, however, represents the valuation of Bruton’s equity rather than the gross value of its vessels. The takeover follows a major restructuring of Trøim’s tanker interests. Bruton originally built up a 12-ship VLCC programme before splitting the business in August, retaining its first four New Times ships and transferring another eight newbuildings into separately listed OMC Tankers. The demerger left Bruton with a concentrated fleet of near-term deliveries, substantial charter cover and financing arrangements with Chinese lessors covering 85% to 90% of construction costs. The eight vessels in OMC Tankers are not part of the International Seaways transaction. For International Seaways, the acquisition continues an aggressive fleet renewal programme that has seen the company dispose of older tonnage while selectively investing in younger ships. The US owner had a fleet of around 70 vessels, including newbuildings, before the deal. It sold seven older tankers, including two VLCCs, earlier this year for more than $216m and has also invested in LR1 newbuildings at South Korea’s K Shipbuilding. The company strengthened its crude tanker trading platform in January by taking full ownership of Tankers International, which subsequently expanded into the suezmax market. The latest acquisition comes against an exceptionally strong earnings backdrop. Alongside the takeover announcement, International Seaways unveiled preliminary third-quarter net income of $340m to $350m, including a roughly $50m gain from the sale of a suezmax. It reported liquidity of approximately $965m at the end of September. The transaction also brings together businesses associated with two familiar names in Norwegian shipping. Family trusts established by John Fredriksen, Trøim’s former longtime business partner, hold a 13.54% stake in International Seaways, according to the latest US regulatory filing. The pair went their separate ways in 2014 after nearly two decades working together. Bruton’s board has unanimously recommended the transaction, with a shareholder vote expected around October 30. Completion is targeted for early November, subject to the necessary approvals, after which Bruton intends to delist from Euronext Growth Oslo. articles.body: Africa Dry Cargo West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada Sam Chambers October 16, 2026 0 2,416 3 minutes read Winning Winning West Africa is fast becoming dry bulk shipping’s biggest growth engine, with its mineral export boom poised to absorb the equivalent of another 120 capesizes by 2030. UK consultancy Tradeviews forecasts in a new report that shipments from the region will surge 50% from 2025 levels to 303m tonnes by the end of the decade, with Guinea’s giant Simandou iron ore project leading the charge. Crucially for shipowners, the long voyages to China will magnify the impact on vessel demand. “West Africa looks set to remain the fastest growing long-haul source of dry bulk cargo,” Tradeviews stated. The growth is already evident. The five West African exporters covered by the consultancy shipped 160.1m tonnes in their principal trades during the first eight months of this year, up 25% year on year. Liberian iron ore exports nearly doubled to 10.1m tonnes. Tradeviews expects regional exports to reach 267m tonnes next year, with Guinean iron ore shipments climbing to 45m tonnes in 2027 and approximately 112m tonnes by 2030. Bauxite exports, meanwhile, are forecast to retreat from a peak of nearly 194m tonnes this year to 153m tonnes by 2030 as Guinea pushes ahead with domestic alumina processing. A capesize round voyage between Guinea and China takes approximately 78 days, compared with just 29 days on the Australia-China route. Tradeviews calculates that moving a tonne from West Africa consequently absorbs around 2.6 times as much vessel time. On this basis, the consultancy estimates West African trades will require the equivalent of 330 capesizes by 2030, compared with 210 last year. There are, however, already signs that the region’s growth ambitions are running up against freight market realities. In its latest weekly report, BRS Shipbrokers noted that exceptionally high freight rates had priced some higher-cost Guinean bauxite miners out of the export market. Guinea shipped 15.61m tonnes of bauxite in September, down 12% from August, with freight costs at one point accounting for more than half the delivered value of the commodity. The subsequent easing in capesize rates could provide some relief. The C3 benchmark has fallen from $43.43 a tonne in late September to $32.95 on October 12, prompting BRS to suggest Guinean bauxite exports could recover by 5% to 10% month on month during November and December. The broker described the situation as a “test of elasticity” rather than the start of another cargo boom, pointing out that Shandong alumina refineries processing imported ore lost RMB261.8 per tonne in September. SSY has similarly warned that Guinean bauxite exports have retreated from early-September highs, observing that “shipping demand is turning more sensitive to margin levels on the mining side”. Tradeviews did also caution that potential Guinean bauxite export restrictions, Simandou project delays, dedicated ore carriers and the displacement of Australian iron ore shipments could reduce the benefits for the wider capesize market with much of the market increasingly looking like a Chinese conveyor belt. SSY noted in a market report from August that VLOCs of more than 220,000 dwt accounted for nearly half of Simandou shipments during the first half of 2026. More significant for independent owners is what is coming down the slipways. SSY data shows Chinese tonnage accounts for nearly 40% of the current VLOC orderbook, raising questions over how much of Simandou’s enormous prospective tonne-mile demand will ultimately filter through to the conventional capesize spot market. Bauxite’s growing importance to dry bulk shipping will be reflected at next April’s Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, with a standalone Bauxite Blitz session. Scheduled for April 28, the discussion will examine the expanding trade, shifting supply patterns and implications for future capesize demand. Confirmed speakers include Ernst Meyer, president and CEO of Torvald Klaveness, and Robert Haggquist, charterer and decarbonisation lead at South32. Braemar’s Derek Langston will moderate the session. articles.title: ScottishPower Renewables completes ‘record-breaking’ cable landfall operation
articles.summary: ScottishPower Renewables has completed what it says was a record-breaking cable landfall operation for its 960 MW East Anglia Two offshore wind...
articles.body: Subsea October 16, 2026 · 2 days ago ScottishPower Renewables completes ‘record-breaking’ cable landfall operation 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email ScottishPower Renewables ScottishPower Renewables has completed what it says was a record-breaking cable landfall operation for its 960 MW East Anglia Two offshore wind farm in the UK, installing two nearly 1.8-kilometer-long ducts beneath the Suffolk coastline and seabed for the project’s export cables. The ducts, each measuring 800 millimeters in diameter, were installed using horizontal directional drilling (HDD), a technique that creates an underground passage without excavating beaches or disturbing the coastline directly. ScottishPower Renewables says the operation involved the world’s longest continuous single sections of extruded polyethylene (PE) ducts and represents the largest electricity transmission landfall of its kind in the UK, based on the combination of duct length and diameter. Manufactured by Pipelife in Norway, the ducts were produced as single uninterrupted lengths, eliminating the need for welded joints. They will provide a protected route for the high-voltage export cables carrying electricity from the offshore wind farm to shore. The landfall works form part of the project’s onshore civil engineering program, led by OCU Group with support from its subsidiary Peter McCormack & Sons. ScottishPower Renewables said the operation also marked a manufacturing record for Pipelife, whose ducts measured approximately 1,793 meters each. “The completion of this colossal HDD, which is three times the length of our other East Anglia projects, is a huge achievement – quite literally – and a major milestone as we progress construction of our third windfarm in the region,” said Ross Ovens , ScottishPower Renewables’ Managing Director for Offshore. “Landfall works are known to be one of the most technically challenging aspects of building an offshore windfarm, but thanks to precision planning and a great partnership with our principal contactor OCU Group and duct manufacturer Pipelife, this programme has well and truly hit the mark – breaking UK and world records in the process.” The milestone comes as East Anglia Two advances towards offshore construction, with the first export cable expected to be installed in summer 2027, and commercial operation targeted for late 2028. The 960 MW offshore wind farm will be built at a site in the southern North Sea, around 33 kilometers off the Suffolk coast at its nearest point, where 64 Siemens Gamesa SG 14-236 DD wind turbines will be installed on monopile foundations. articles.body: Asia Containers HMM commits $1.6bn to 12 more containerships Sam Chambers October 16, 2026 0 1,964 1 minute read HMM HMM South Korea’s HMM is pressing ahead with its fleet expansion programme, approving a $1.62bn investment in 12 containerships comprising eight 13,000 teu newbuildings and four smaller vessels. The Seoul-listed carrier’s board approved spending KRW2.168trn ($1.617bn) yesterday, according to a stock exchange filing. The investment includes fresh orders for eight 13,000 teu ships, alongside the acquisition of three 2,800 teu vessels and one 1,700 teu ship through resale transactions involving newbuildings already under construction. The 12 vessels will add a combined 114,100 teu of capacity, with deliveries scheduled to be completed by December 2029. HMM has yet to identify the shipyards responsible for the eight larger vessels or the sellers of the four smaller ships. Propulsion specifications have also not been disclosed. The latest investment follows last year’s KRW4trn ($2.8bn) commitment covering 12 LNG dual-fuel 13,000 teu containerships and two VLCCs, with HD Hyundai and Hanwha Ocean securing the boxship contracts. Under HMM’s business plan through to 2030, the carrier aims to expand its containership fleet to 166 vessels totalling 1.47m teu by the end of the decade, alongside 110 bulk carriers with a combined capacity of 13.52m dwt. articles.body: Europe Greater China Shipyards Tankers Liquimar lines up suezmax trio at New Hantong Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 803 1 minute read Liquimar Liquimar Greek tanker owner Liquimar Tankers has been linked to an order for three suezmax newbuildings in China, adding fresh crude carrier capacity after cashing in on the strong secondhand tanker market. The Dimitris Papadimitriou-controlled company has contracted three 157,000 dwt vessels at Jiangsu New Hantong Ship Heavy Industry, according to shipbuilding sources. The conventionally fuelled tankers are scheduled for delivery in the second half of 2030, with pricing estimated at just under $86m apiece, putting the potential investment at close to $258m. The move follows Liquimar’s disposal of two ageing suezmaxes, the 2007-built Orpheas and Evridiki , to Dubai-based energy trader Onex DMCC. Liquimar has already emerged behind another Chinese tanker project this year. In August, shipbuilding intelligence identified the company as the owner of the 113,500 dwt aframax/LR2 Priamos under construction at Hengli Heavy Industries. That vessel marked the Athens-based owner’s return to newbuilding activity after a lengthy absence. Liquimar was set up in 1990, as a way for its parent company, Dioryx Maritime Corp, to expand from dry cargo and containerships into the oil tanker sector, before becoming a standalone entity in 1995. The latest reported deal would add another name to New Hantong’s suezmax orderbook. articles.title: GSI taps bridge builder to ease ship block bottleneck
articles.summary: Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) has turned to one of China’s oldest bridge builders for outsourced hull block construction, joining a growing number of shipyards tapping manufacturers outside the traditional maritime supply chain to keep pace with swelling orderbooks. articles.body: Greater China Shipyards GSI taps bridge builder to ease ship block bottleneck Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 430 2 minutes read GSI GSI Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) has turned to one of China’s oldest bridge builders for outsourced hull block construction, joining a growing number of shipyards tapping manufacturers outside the traditional maritime supply chain to keep pace with swelling orderbooks. The CSSC-controlled yard has signed a framework agreement with China Railway Shanhaiguan Bridge Group, bringing the heavy-steel fabricator into its shipbuilding operations. GSI said its expanding orderbook and increasingly complex vessel mix would drive up demand for hull blocks over the coming years, prompting the move to bring in additional manufacturing capacity. Shanhaiguan, founded in 1894, specialises in bridge steel structures and railway equipment and operates six production bases across China. Under the agreement, it will allocate fabrication resources to ship blocks and take responsibility for production quality, safety and delivery schedules. Neither the contract value nor the volume of work has been disclosed. The agreement comes with GSI’s production schedule already stretching towards the end of the decade. The Guangzhou-based builder disclosed earlier this year that its contracted business was approaching RMB100bn ($14bn), with overseas orders accounting for more than 95% and construction slots extending into 2030. Its most recent intake includes 10 MR tankers ordered by Greek owner Evangelos Pistiolis’ Central Group, four additional MR vessels for Advantage Tankers and more LNG dual-fuel car carriers for MSC-controlled Global Car Carriers. GSI is also expanding its physical footprint. In May, it signed a joint venture agreement with Guangdong Port and Shipping Group to develop the 360,000 sq m Xiaohudao shipbuilding base in Guangzhou. A separate project launched in September will see a new facility built at Longxue North, with GSI lined up to operate the yard once completed in 2029. The latter is designed to produce up to 18 vessels annually. The Shanhaiguan deal is not an isolated move. Several Chinese bridge and structural-steel manufacturers have entered shipbuilding this year, taking on fabrication work previously handled by established yards. In June, China Railway Baoji Bridge Group’s Yangzhou subsidiary began manufacturing hull sections for a 73,000 dwt self-propelled deck carrier. The project involves 110 blocks across the vessel’s cargo section, with the largest weighing about 190 tonnes. Jingjiang Nanyang Shipbuilding is providing construction coordination, with China Classification Society overseeing technical and quality requirements. Another bridge specialist, Jingjiang Heavy Industry, followed in September, starting work on blocks for a 40,400 dwt bulk carrier. The China Railway Construction Corporation subsidiary is fabricating 10 cargo-hold bottom sections weighing up to 96 tonnes each, which are to be transported to Shanghai for final assembly. The company has established three outdoor block assembly lines and is targeting annual ship block production of up to 100,000 tonnes, with longer-term ambitions to move into complete vessel construction. Other Chinese shipbuilders have opted to expand fabrication capacity closer to home. Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding commissioned an expansion of its curved-block workshop in late 2025, adding nearly 23,000 sq m of production space. Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding also proposed a new block fabrication and assembly facility last year to address capacity constraints and reduce its reliance on external subcontractors. The moves form part of a broader capacity buildout across China. Broker BRS Group identified at least seven dormant shipyards being reactivated and a further dozen established facilities expanding production capacity, developments covered by Splash earlier this year. South Korean builders have been taking similar steps to overcome production bottlenecks. In April, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries introduced a split-hull construction method for a 157,000 dwt suezmax, outsourcing the 168 m bow section to HSG Sungdong Shipbuilding before joining it to a stern section built at Ulsan. HJ Shipbuilding & Construction has also shifted work outside its Yeongdo yard, contracting Daesun Shipbuilding in February to manufacture deckhouse blocks for eight 7,900 teu containerships after its own facilities reached capacity. articles.title: Shipping’s AI winners will build capability, not buy technology
articles.summary: The technology is already widely available. The advantage will come from how shipping companies turn it into specialised systems, define its place in the team and manage adoption, says Michalis Gkontas, co-founder and CEO of AskChief. Today’s AI systems can already perform useful knowledge work. They can search and...
articles.body: Contributions Tech Shipping’s AI winners will build capability, not buy technology Splash October 16, 2026 0 479 3 minutes read Gerd Altmann via Pixabay Gerd Altmann via Pixabay The technology is already widely available. The advantage will come from how shipping companies turn it into specialised systems, define its place in the team and manage adoption, says Michalis Gkontas, co-founder and CEO of AskChief. Today’s AI systems can already perform useful knowledge work. They can search and interpret large volumes of information, compare documents, prepare drafts and help people work through complex tasks. The more important question now is whether organisations are ready to deploy them well. Giving employees access to a general-purpose AI tool is easy. Turning that access into better technical work, stronger compliance and additional team capacity is a management challenge. Leaders must decide where AI should be used, what knowledge it can draw on and where professional responsibility remains. Access is not capability As connectivity improves across fleets, many seafarers can access the same general-purpose AI tools as colleagues ashore, whether or not their company has formally deployed them. A report or proposed response may arrive in polished language without showing what evidence supports it, which company procedure applies or how much was generated by AI. Fluent output is not necessarily useful output. Generic AI can make weak reasoning look convincing or produce material that does not fit the vessel’s actual circumstances. The shore team must then reconstruct the context and verify the basis of what it has received. A generic model does not naturally know which version of a company’s safety management system is current, whether a manual applies to the equipment fitted on a particular vessel or who must approve a proposed SMS change. Specialisation comes from the system built around the model: the company’s knowledge, role-specific instructions, specialist tools, established workflows, permissions and review points. The underlying model may be general-purpose. The operational system should not be. Begin with work that matters The weakest deployment brief is simply to “use AI more”. It leaves each employee to decide what the technology is for, which information is appropriate to use and how much confidence to place in the result. A stronger starting point is a recurring piece of work the team already understands: investigating a technical issue, preparing for an inspection, answering an SMS question or assessing how a new requirement affects company procedures. The task should be meaningful enough to matter but bounded enough to manage. Once the team sees AI supporting a familiar workflow, expansion becomes an operational decision rather than an abstract technology initiative. Let AI do the work around the decision AI is well suited to locating relevant material, assembling context, comparing records, identifying potential gaps and preparing a first draft. People remain responsible for interpreting the evidence, challenging its relevance, resolving uncertainty and approving the action. Its purpose is not to diminish professional expertise, but to extend its reach. A useful shorthand is the 10-80-10 rule. It is not a literal allocation of time or effort, but a sequence for organising the work. In the first 10%, the expert defines the problem, supplies the context and sets the standard for a good outcome. AI carries much of the middle 80% by finding information, structuring it, comparing records and preparing the work. In the final 10%, the accountable professional challenges the result, corrects it and decides what happens next. The percentages should change with the risk. A safety-critical decision may require far more human review than a routine summary. Make adoption a team practice Leaders need to set expectations, appoint owners and create simple feedback loops. Teams should be able to share useful cases, flag weak outputs, and show where information or workflow design needs improvement. In shipping, caution is usually rational. A confident but incorrect answer can waste time or introduce risk. Trust grows when users can inspect the underlying evidence, understand the system’s boundaries and see that their professional judgement remains central. The same discipline should shape measurement. Logins and prompts reveal little. Better questions are whether the team reached a reviewed outcome faster, used relevant company history, avoided duplicate work and captured the decision for the next person. Deployment will create the advantage AI models will keep becoming more powerful and widely available. Access will not be scarce, and it will not provide a durable advantage on its own. The difference will come from deployment: choosing the right work, building specialised systems around it and helping teams incorporate those systems into everyday operations. For leaders, this means treating AI neither as a standalone IT purchase nor as an instruction to reduce headcount. It is an opportunity to give capable people better tools and increase what the organisation can accomplish without weakening accountability. The technology exists. The management challenge is to turn it into a working organisational capability. The shipping companies that do this well will not simply have more people using AI. They will have better-equipped teams, stronger company knowledge and more capacity to act.
